author: A Robot
objectives: Describe Mars’s apparent retrograde motion during a ∼26-month cycle: eastward drift, slowing/halting, westward loop, and return to eastward motion.
Explain, using heliocentric relative motion, why Earth overtakes a slower outer planet to produce an apparent backward loop.
Compare geocentric and heliocentric explanations and articulate why the heliocentric model is more parsimonious.
Predict when retrograde motion will occur for a given outer planet based on the relative geometry between Earth and that planet.
Compare retrograde loop sizes for Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn and explain why more distant planets produce smaller loops.

modules.description: Observe Mars over a fast-forward interval and identify eastward drift, retrograde loop, and return.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Track Mars’s apparent motion against labeled constellations over time.
Describe the sequence: eastward drift → slowdown/stop → westward loop (~15°) → resumption eastward motion.
Distinguish apparent motion across the sky from actual changes in Mars’s direction.
instructions: Allow the scene to play. Watch Mars relative to the labeled ecliptic constellations.
Use the trail to estimate the total loop extent (~15°).

clips.changeMeaning: In the night-sky scene, Earth is visible with a starfield backdrop. Mars and a faint retrograde trail are enabled so students can track the apparent path against labeled constellations.
clips.narration: Retrograde motion is the puzzle: when an outer planet like Mars seems to pause, then move backward across the constellations, before resuming its usual eastward drift.

clips.changeMeaning: Mars’s on-sky position shifts slightly eastward (left in the viewer’s perspective), and the trail appends a short segment to begin the full loop visualization.
clips.narration: For the first stretch, Mars drifts slowly eastward relative to the stars. Watch how the red point moves while the constellations remain fixed.

clips.changeMeaning: Mars slows and nearly halts near the loop’s turning point; its marker slightly increases for visual emphasis while the trail adds the final pre-reversal segment.
clips.narration: Then Mars slows, nearly stops, and begins moving westward. That apparent reversal happens without Mars making a dramatic course change.

clips.changeMeaning: Mars moves westward across the labeled field and the trail grows along the retrograde portion, making the loop’s arc evident.
clips.narration: Over roughly two months, Mars traces a westward loop across the sky—about 15 degrees in apparent angular extent.

clips.changeMeaning: Mars returns to eastward drift as the trail completes the loop. The finalized trail reinforces the full retrograde path students observed.
clips.narration: Finally Mars slows again, reverses back, and resumes eastward motion. The completed trail shows the whole retrograde loop.

modules.description: Build a Ptolemaic-style epicycle/deferent system and see how combined circular motions produce retrograde appearance.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify the deferent (large circle centered on Earth) and epicycle (small circle riding on deferent).
Explain how retrograde appearance arises when Mars is on the near side of the epicycle relative to Earth.
Describe why this model requires tuned parameters and more epicycles for accuracy.
instructions: Watch the epicycle path and focus on the configuration that produces apparent westward motion.
Compare the epicycle’s combined motion to the resulting apparent motion from Earth.

clips.changeMeaning: Earth-centered deferent and epicycle are displayed with Mars riding the epicycle. The retrograde indicator stays hidden until the configuration demonstrates apparent backward motion.
clips.narration: In the geocentric model, Mars rides on an epicycle, which moves along a larger deferent centered on Earth.

clips.changeMeaning: Mars is placed on a configuration that produces apparent eastward drift while the retrograde indicator remains off.
clips.narration: Most of the time, the combined circular motions make Mars appear to drift eastward across the sky.

clips.changeMeaning: Mars reaches the epicycle’s near side relative to Earth in the diagram; the retrograde indicator turns on and flips to show apparent westward motion.
clips.narration: When Mars reaches the near side of the epicycle—closest to Earth—its combined motion makes it appear to move westward.

clips.changeMeaning: The diagram advances so the epicycle point traces the retrograde segment; Mars is emphasized to help students track the apparent loop driver.
clips.narration: As the epicycle continues, the apparent backward motion forms a loop—but getting the details right required carefully tuned parameters and additional epicycles.

modules.moduleName: Scene 3: Heliocentric View Outside the Solar System
modules.description: Show Sun-centered orbits for Earth and Mars with correct relative speeds to produce retrograde without epicycles.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Use relative orbital speeds to explain when Earth overtakes Mars (~every 26 months).
Describe how Earth overtaking Mars produces an apparent loop in the line-of-sight.
Contrast smooth heliocentric orbits with the epicycle mechanism.
instructions: Watch Earth and Mars move around the Sun. Retrograde appears as an apparent effect from the changing relative geometry.
Relate the overtake moment to what students saw in Scene 1.

clips.changeMeaning: Heliocentric orbits are initialized with Earth on the 1 AU orbit and Mars on the 1.52 AU orbit; the retrograde marker starts hidden.
clips.narration: From outside the solar system, Earth and Mars move on smooth orbits. Retrograde motion is an apparent effect that appears when Earth overtakes Mars.

clips.changeMeaning: Earth moves to a position inside Mars’s orbit while Mars lags behind; the retrograde marker turns on to emphasize the overtake/retrograde-producing geometry.
clips.narration: Roughly every 26 months, Earth catches up on its faster inner track. That overtake geometry is what produces the apparent westward loop.

clips.changeMeaning: Earth and Mars are gently emphasized while the retrograde marker color shifts to reinforce that no epicycles are required to generate the loop.
clips.narration: Notice: we didn’t stack epicycles. Two smooth orbits produce the loop naturally through relative motion.

modules.moduleName: Scene 4: Linking Outside View to Night-sky Line-of-sight
modules.description: Side-by-side linkage: show a line of sight from Earth through Mars to the starfield as Earth overtakes Mars.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Relate outside-system overtake geometry to apparent reversal in the night sky.
Explain that the loop is real apparent motion driven by geometry.
Describe how line-of-sight sweeps eastward then westward and retraces its path.
instructions: Watch the line-of-sight sweep. When it reverses, Mars’s apparent position should trace back across the starfield.
Track Mars continuously—there is no real stop in Mars’s physical orbit.

components.text: Line of sight: Earth → Mars → stars

clips.changeMeaning: The side-by-side linkage begins: Earth and Mars define the outside geometry, and the starfield shows Mars’s apparent position updated by the line of sight.
clips.narration: Let’s connect the outside view to the night sky. As Earth moves, draw a line of sight through Mars to the background stars.

clips.changeMeaning: Earth advances along its orbit while Mars remains briefly ahead; the line-of-sight sweeps east across the starfield and the apparent Mars point shifts accordingly.
clips.narration: During normal motion, the line of sight sweeps eastward through the constellations, and Mars’s apparent position drifts east.

clips.changeMeaning: As Earth begins to overtake Mars, the line-of-sight direction reverses and Mars’s apparent point moves westward across the starfield, reproducing retrograde motion.
clips.narration: When Earth starts to overtake Mars, the line of sight reverses. At that moment, the apparent Mars position retraces—retrograde motion.

clips.changeMeaning: After Earth passes Mars, the line-of-sight sweeps eastward again and Mars’s apparent position resumes its eastward drift, completing the loop linkage.
clips.narration: Once Earth has passed Mars, the line resumes its eastward sweep and Mars’s apparent motion follows. The loop comes from geometry.

modules.description: Students walk around a small inner orbit while keeping gaze on Mars, generating an apparent retrograde loop.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Demonstrate how observer motion relative to a background produces apparent backward motion.
Generate and describe the retrograde sequence from a human perspective.
Connect the overtaking action to the apparent loop.
instructions: Move along the inner floor ring slowly while keeping your gaze fixed on Mars.
Watch for the moment when Mars appears to move backward relative to the starfield.

components.text: Walk the inner circle while keeping your gaze on Mars

clips.changeMeaning: The embodied experiment starts: the floor ring marks the observer’s inner motion, Mars stays fixed in the distance, and a faint trail visualizes the apparent path.
clips.narration: Here’s the key idea: retrograde motion is what you see when your own motion changes the line of sight to a farther target.

clips.changeMeaning: As the learner begins moving around the inner ring, the trail shows an apparent eastward drift generated by observer motion.
clips.narration: At first, as you move along the inner track, Mars appears to drift east across the background stars.

clips.changeMeaning: Near the closest-approach configuration, the apparent direction reverses; the trail highlights the turning point to mirror retrograde onset.
clips.narration: When you pass the closest-approach position, Mars appears to move backward—retrograde.

clips.changeMeaning: The learner completes the loop: the trail continues past reversal and finishes the retrograde pattern, after which the motion would resume its original drift direction.
clips.narration: Finish the walk around the circle to complete the apparent loop. The pattern arises from relative motion—just like Earth overtaking Mars.

modules.moduleName: Scene 6: Compare Mars vs Jupiter vs Saturn
modules.description: Heliocentric view showing loop sizes for multiple outer planets and explaining why loops shrink with distance.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Compare apparent retrograde loop sizes: Mars (~15°), Jupiter (~10°), Saturn (~7°).
Explain why more distant planets yield smaller apparent loops.
Relate this trend to subtended-angle geometry similar to parallax.
instructions: Use the arc markers to gauge loop sizes for each planet.
Observe the trend: farther planets produce smaller, less dramatic loops.

components.text:
Loop size trend:
Mars ~15° • Jupiter ~10° • Saturn ~7°

clips.changeMeaning: Arc markers for Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn are enabled to set up a consistent comparison of loop extents.
clips.narration: Let’s compare retrograde loops across outer planets. The key trend is that loops get smaller as distance from the Sun increases.

clips.changeMeaning: Mars is emphasized and its ~15° arc is visually highlighted while Jupiter and Saturn arcs are dimmed for focus.
clips.narration: Mars produces the most dramatic loop—around 15 degrees across.

clips.changeMeaning: The focus shifts to Jupiter, whose ~10° loop arc is highlighted while the others are dimmed.
clips.narration: Jupiter’s loop is smaller—about 10 degrees—because the relative geometry subtends a smaller apparent angle.

clips.changeMeaning: Saturn is emphasized and its smallest (~7°) arc is highlighted, completing the comparison trend.
clips.narration: Saturn’s loop is smallest—near 7 degrees. Farther planets show less dramatic retrograde because Earth’s inner motion creates a smaller angular effect.

modules.description: Manipulate Earth and Mars configurations; use an inset to determine whether retrograde will be observed from Earth.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Predict retrograde onset by placing the outer planet near the geometrical condition for Earth to overtake.
Interpret how changing Earth’s orbital phase shifts the retrograde window.
Verify predictions using an inset night-sky retrograde indicator.
instructions: Drag Mars around its orbit handle.
Watch the inset: when Mars is placed correctly, the retrograde indicator appears and the apparent loop is shown.
Repeat after moving Earth to a new phase.

components.text:
Goal: place Mars near the arc where Earth is about to overtake
(near opposition) so the inset shows retrograde.

clips.changeMeaning: The prediction challenge begins: the inset retrograde indicator is hidden initially, and Mars is ready to be dragged.
clips.narration: Now you’ll predict when retrograde motion will be observed. The inset simulates what an observer on Earth would see.

clips.changeMeaning: Earth is placed at orbital configuration A; students must adjust Mars to find the shifted retrograde window.
clips.narration: First, fix Earth at position A. Drag Mars and watch for the retrograde loop to appear in the inset.

clips.changeMeaning: Mars is positioned near the geometrical condition that produces Earth overtaking soon; the inset retrograde indicator turns on and the apparent Mars point shifts accordingly.
clips.narration: When Mars is placed near the correct arc—close to opposition—the inset shows the retrograde loop. Your prediction matches the geometry.

clips.changeMeaning: Earth moves to a new orbital configuration B, disabling the previous retrograde indication; students must find the new retrograde window by relocating Mars.
clips.narration: Now move to Earth position B. The retrograde window shifts—again, it’s the relative configuration that matters.

modules.description: Summarize the key concept areas covered during the lab.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Integrate observed retrograde phenomenon with geocentric and heliocentric explanations.
Explain why heliocentrism is favored on grounds of parsimony.
Describe how geometry links outside-system overtaking to inside-view line-of-sight reversal.
Compare loop sizes across outer planets.
instructions: Review each highlighted concept area. When the narration references a concept, recall the corresponding scene.

components.text: AR Lab Recap: Apparent Retrograde Motion
4) Link outside geometry to night-sky line-of-sight

clips.changeMeaning: The checklist appears with the observation item visually emphasized first.
clips.narration: First, recall the observed phenomenon: Mars drifts eastward, slows, makes a westward loop, then returns to eastward motion.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight shifts to the geocentric epicycle explanation to connect the loop to deferent and epicycle machinery.
clips.narration: Second, the geocentric model uses deferent and epicycle machinery. It can reproduce the loop, but it depends on tuned parameters and more epicycles as data improves.

clips.changeMeaning: Emphasis moves to heliocentric resolution: smooth Earth and Mars orbits generate retrograde through relative overtaking geometry.
clips.narration: Third, heliocentrism resolves retrograde more simply: Earth moves faster on its inner orbit and overtakes Mars about every 26 months.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight shifts to viewpoint linkage between the outside system and the inside night-sky line of sight.
clips.narration: Fourth, we linked viewpoints: as Earth approaches and passes Mars, the line of sight sweeps eastward then westward, making Mars retrace its apparent path.

clips.changeMeaning: The final checklist item is emphasized, tying reduced loop size to distance and subtended-angle geometry.
clips.narration: Finally, compare outer planets: Mars shows the largest loop, Jupiter a smaller one, and Saturn the smallest, because distance reduces the apparent angular effect.
